newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo Republic unrest spreads, mortars hit Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Congo Republic unrest spreads, mortars hit Kinshasa.

text.p: Fighting in the Congo Republic, until now largely confined to the capital Brazzaville, spread to the interior and spilled briefly across the border into the former Zaire, witnesses and aid workers said on Thursday.

Aid workers said clashes between forces loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and supporters of his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso broke out on Sunday in Impfondo, about 900 km (560 miles) north of Brazzaville.
A radio station controlled by Lissouba accused Sassou's troops of launching the attack.
Aid workers, citing radio messages from church sources, said there may have been renewed fighting on Tuesday in Impfondo.

In another development in the Congo conflict, two mortar bombs presumably fired from Brazzaville landed across the Congo River border in Kinshasa, capital of the recently renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire).
"One of the shells landed in the garden of a primary school near the foreign ministry," a witness said. The second fell in the middle of an empty road.
There was no injury or material damage from the incidents.
Earlier on Thursday, state radio in Kinshasa said President Laurent Kabila's troops retaliated with mortar fire into Brazzaville after shells were fired from there on Tuesday.
Meanwhile hundreds of refugees crossed into Kinshasa on Thursday, fleeing a flareup in the ethnic and political unrest that has gripped Brazzaville since June.
Refugees crossing the Congo River said they were mainly from Brazzaville's Poto-Poto quarter, once a thriving market district and now the object of intense shelling.

They were arriving at Kinshasa's main passenger landing stage, known as Ngobila Beach, in dugouts and boats. Those wounded in the fighting were transferred by the Red Cross to two hospitals in Kinshasa.
Aid workers said the northern area around Impfondo where fighting had spread is normally sparsely populated.

However, in the past four months it has filled up with Rwandan Hutu refugees who trekked across the former Zaire fleeing the advance of Kabila's rebel troops as they advanced to seize power in Kinshasa in May.
Aid workers fear there may have been numerous casualties among the Rwandans around Impfondo.

"The military operations haven't been directed against the refugees, but there were a lot of them around that site," said one aid worker with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Kinshasa.
Lissouba's radio reported the refugees, who count members of the former Rwandan Hutu army in their ranks, had been fighting alongside Sassou. But no independent confirmation was available.
Throughout the conflict, rival radios have accused the opposing side of using foreign troops and mercenaries.
The fighting has forced the indefinite postponement of presidential elections last month in which both Lissouba and Sassou were to be candidates.
Efforts to mediate an end to the conflict have been stalled by arguments over the appointment of an interim prime minister and what powers he should have.
Well over two thousand people were killed in militia warfare in Brazzaville following disputes over elections in 1993.
The latest unrest has killed hundreds and devastated whole districts of Brazzaville.
